**Jean-Loup Jacques Marie Chrétien** (born 20 August 1938) is a French retired _Général de Brigade_ (brigadier general) in the _[Armée de l'Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_Air\_and\_Space\_Force "French Air and Space Force")_ (French air force), and a former [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES")[spationaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He flew on two Franco-Soviet space missions and a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission. Chrétien was the first Frenchman and the first western European in space.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Chrétien was born in the town of [La Rochelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Rochelle "La Rochelle"), France. He was married to and then divorced from Amy Kristine Jensen of [New Canaan, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Canaan,_Connecticut "New Canaan, Connecticut"), and had five children. His father, Jacques, was a Navy sailor, and his mother, the former Marie-Blanche Coudurier, was a housewife. Chrétien is fluent in French, English and Russian.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

Chrétien was educated at the École communale in [Ploujean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ploujean "Ploujean"), the Collège Saint-Charles in [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), and the Lycée de [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix"). He entered the [École de l'Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_de_l'air_et_de_l'espace "École de l'air et de l'espace") (the French Air Force Academy) at [Salon-de-Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon-de-Provence "Salon-de-Provence") and graduated in 1961, receiving a master's degree in aeronautical engineering.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Career")]

Chrétien received his fighter pilot/pilot-engineer wings in 1962, after one year of training on [Mystère IVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Myst%C3%A8re_IV "Dassault Mystère IV"). He was promoted to lieutenant, and joined the 5th Fighter Wing in Orange, in the southeast of France, where he served for seven years as a fighter pilot in an operational squadron flying [Super-Mystere B2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Super_Myst%C3%A8re "Dassault Super Mystère") and then [Mirage III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_III "Dassault Mirage III") interceptors. In 1970, he was assigned to the French test pilots school, EPNER ([École du personnel navigant d'essais et de réception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_du_personnel_navigant_d'essais_et_de_r%C3%A9ception "École du personnel navigant d'essais et de réception")), then served as a test pilot at the [Istres-Le Tubé Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istres-Le_Tub%C3%A9_Air_Base "Istres-Le Tubé Air Base") for seven years. During that time he was responsible for supervising the flight test program for the [Mirage F-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_F1 "Dassault Mirage F1") fighter. In 1977–1978, he was appointed deputy commander of the South Air Defence Division in [Aix-en-Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aix-en-Provence "Aix-en-Provence"), and he served in this position until his selection as a [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") in June 1980. Chrétien remained a French Air Force officer but was placed on detachment to [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES") for his space flight activities ensuring his availability for future flights with the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") (NASA), [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") ([Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")) or [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") ([ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency")). He has accumulated over 8,000 hours of flying time in various aircraft, including [Tupolev-154](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupolev_Tu-154 "Tupolev Tu-154"), [MiG-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikoyan-Gurevich_MiG-25 "Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25"), [Sukhoi Su-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-26 "Sukhoi Su-26"), and [Sukhoi Su-27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-27 "Sukhoi Su-27"). A veteran of three space flights, Chrétien was the tenth [Interkosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interkosmos "Interkosmos") cosmonaut, and has spent a total of 43 days, 11 hours, 18 minutes, 42 seconds in space, including an [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) of 5 hours, 57 minutes.

In April 1979, the Soviet Union offered France the opportunity to fly a cosmonaut on board a joint Soviet-French space flight, along the same lines as the agreement to fly non-Soviet cosmonauts from member countries of the Interkosmos program. The offer was accepted, and France began a spationaut selection process in September 1979. Chrétien was one of two finalists named on 12 June 1980. He started training at the [Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center") in September 1980. The following year, he was named as the research cosmonaut for the prime crew of the [Soyuz T-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6 "Soyuz T-6") mission.

Soyuz T-6 was launched on 24 June 1982, and Chrétien, [Vladimir Dzhanibekov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Dzhanibekov "Vladimir Dzhanibekov") and [Aleksandr Ivanchenkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Ivanchenkov "Aleksandr Ivanchenkov") linked up with [Salyut 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_7 "Salyut 7") and joined the crew of [Anatoli Berezovoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Berezovoy "Anatoli Berezovoy") and [Valentin Lebedev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_Lebedev "Valentin Lebedev") already on board. They spent nearly seven days carrying out a program of joint Soviet-French experiments, including a series of French echography cardiovascular monitoring system experiments, before returning to Earth after a flight lasting 7 days, 21 hours, 50 minutes, and 42 seconds. This flight made him the first Western non-American to go to space, as well as the first Western European. Following the mission he was appointed chief of the CNES Astronaut Office.

Chrétien was selected as the back-up crew member for [STS-51-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G "STS-51-G") ([Patrick Baudry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Baudry "Patrick Baudry"), another CNES astronaut, flew on that mission). During 1984–1985, he participated in mission training at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center").

Chrétien made his second space flight as a research cosmonaut on board [Soyuz TM-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-7 "Soyuz TM-7"), which launched on 26 November 1988. Together with [Alexander Alexandrovich Volkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Alexandrovich_Volkov_(cosmonaut) "Alexander Alexandrovich Volkov (cosmonaut)") and [Sergei Krikalev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Krikalev "Sergei Krikalev"), he linked up with Mir and joined the crew of [Vladimir Titov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Titov_(cosmonaut) "Vladimir Titov (cosmonaut)"), [Musa Manarov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Manarov "Musa Manarov") and [Valeriy Polyakov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valeriy_Polyakov "Valeriy Polyakov") already on board. They spent 22 days carrying out a program of joint Soviet-French experiments, including a 5-hour and 57-minute EVA by Volkov and Chrétien during which the two men installed the French ERA experimental deployable structure and a panel of material samples. In making the EVA, he became the first non-American and non-Soviet to walk in space. In addition, he was the first non-Soviet cosmonaut to make a second space flight aboard a Soviet spacecraft. The mission lasted 24 days, 18 hours, and 7 minutes.

During 1990–1993, Chrétien participated in [Buran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Buran "Shuttle Buran") spacecraft pilot training at the Moscow Joukovski Institute.

In 1994, he was selected as part of [NASA Astronaut Group 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Group_15 "NASA Astronaut Group 15") to officially become an International Mission Specialist with NASA.

Chrétien attended ASCAN Training at the Johnson Space Center during 1995. He was initially assigned to work on technical issues for the Operations Planning Branch of the Astronaut Office. He served on the crew of [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86")[_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") (25 September to 6 October 1997) the seventh mission to rendezvous and dock with the Russian Space Station Mir. Highlights included the delivery of a Mir [attitude control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_attitude_control "Spacecraft attitude control") computer, the exchange of U.S. crew members [Mike Foale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Foale "Michael Foale") and [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"), a spacewalk by [Scott E. Parazynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski "Scott E. Parazynski") and Vladimir Titov to retrieve four experiments first deployed on Mir during the [STS-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-76 "STS-76") docking mission, the transfer to Mir of 4,700 kg (10,400 lb) of science and logistics, and the return of experiment hardware and results to [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Mission duration was 10 days, 19 hours, and 21 minutes.

In September 2000, while visiting a [Home Depot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Depot "Home Depot") store in [Webster, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webster,_Texas "Webster, Texas"), he was hit by a 31 kg (68 lb) drill press that fell from a shelf more than 3 m (9.8 ft) above him. The injuries to his neck, head, and shoulders were severe enough that a NASA flight surgeon determined that Chrétien could no longer fly. He was forced to retire from the space program in 2001. He filed a US$15 million lawsuit against Home Depot several months after the accident. The company settled the suit in 2002. The terms of the settlement are protected by a confidentiality agreement.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien#cite_note-3) Chrétien is currently working for Tietronix Software as the vice president of research and development in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), Texas.

**Jean-Loup Jacques Marie Chrétien** (born 20 August 1938) is a French retired _Général de Brigade_ (brigadier general) in the _[Armée de l'Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_Air\_and\_Space\_Force "French Air and Space Force")_ (French air force), and a former [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES")[spationaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He flew on two Franco-Soviet space missions and a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission. Chrétien was the first Frenchman and the first western European in space.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Chrétien was born in the town of [La Rochelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Rochelle "La Rochelle"), France. He was married to and then divorced from Amy Kristine Jensen of [New Canaan, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Canaan,_Connecticut "New Canaan, Connecticut"), and had five children. His father, Jacques, was a Navy sailor, and his mother, the former Marie-Blanche Coudurier, was a housewife. Chrétien is fluent in French, English and Russian.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

Chrétien was educated at the École communale in [Ploujean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ploujean "Ploujean"), the Collège Saint-Charles in [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), and the Lycée de [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix"). He entered the [École de l'Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_de_l'air_et_de_l'espace "École de l'air et de l'espace") (the French Air Force Academy) at [Salon-de-Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon-de-Provence "Salon-de-Provence") and graduated in 1961, receiving a master's degree in aeronautical engineering.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Career")]

Chrétien received his fighter pilot/pilot-engineer wings in 1962, after one year of training on [Mystère IVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Myst%C3%A8re_IV "Dassault Mystère IV"). He was promoted to lieutenant, and joined the 5th Fighter Wing in Orange, in the southeast of France, where he served for seven years as a fighter pilot in an operational squadron flying [Super-Mystere B2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Super_Myst%C3%A8re "Dassault Super Mystère") and then [Mirage III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_III "Dassault Mirage III") interceptors. In 1970, he was assigned to the French test pilots school, EPNER ([École du personnel navigant d'essais et de réception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_du_personnel_navigant_d'essais_et_de_r%C3%A9ception "École du personnel navigant d'essais et de réception")), then served as a test pilot at the [Istres-Le Tubé Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istres-Le_Tub%C3%A9_Air_Base "Istres-Le Tubé Air Base") for seven years. During that time he was responsible for supervising the flight test program for the [Mirage F-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_F1 "Dassault Mirage F1") fighter. In 1977–1978, he was appointed deputy commander of the South Air Defence Division in [Aix-en-Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aix-en-Provence "Aix-en-Provence"), and he served in this position until his selection as a [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") in June 1980. Chrétien remained a French Air Force officer but was placed on detachment to [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES") for his space flight activities ensuring his availability for future flights with the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") (NASA), [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") ([Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")) or [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") ([ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency")). He has accumulated over 8,000 hours of flying time in various aircraft, including [Tupolev-154](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupolev_Tu-154 "Tupolev Tu-154"), [MiG-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikoyan-Gurevich_MiG-25 "Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25"), [Sukhoi Su-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-26 "Sukhoi Su-26"), and [Sukhoi Su-27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-27 "Sukhoi Su-27"). A veteran of three space flights, Chrétien was the tenth [Interkosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interkosmos "Interkosmos") cosmonaut, and has spent a total of 43 days, 11 hours, 18 minutes, 42 seconds in space, including an [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) of 5 hours, 57 minutes.

In April 1979, the Soviet Union offered France the opportunity to fly a cosmonaut on board a joint Soviet-French space flight, along the same lines as the agreement to fly non-Soviet cosmonauts from member countries of the Interkosmos program. The offer was accepted, and France began a spationaut selection process in September 1979. Chrétien was one of two finalists named on 12 June 1980. He started training at the [Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center") in September 1980. The following year, he was named as the research cosmonaut for the prime crew of the [Soyuz T-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6 "Soyuz T-6") mission.

Soyuz T-6 was launched on 24 June 1982, and Chrétien, [Vladimir Dzhanibekov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Dzhanibekov "Vladimir Dzhanibekov") and [Aleksandr Ivanchenkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Ivanchenkov "Aleksandr Ivanchenkov") linked up with [Salyut 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_7 "Salyut 7") and joined the crew of [Anatoli Berezovoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Berezovoy "Anatoli Berezovoy") and [Valentin Lebedev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_Lebedev "Valentin Lebedev") already on board. They spent nearly seven days carrying out a program of joint Soviet-French experiments, including a series of French echography cardiovascular monitoring system experiments, before returning to Earth after a flight lasting 7 days, 21 hours, 50 minutes, and 42 seconds. This flight made him the first Western non-American to go to space, as well as the first Western European. Following the mission he was appointed chief of the CNES Astronaut Office.

Chrétien was selected as the back-up crew member for [STS-51-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-G "STS-51-G") ([Patrick Baudry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Baudry "Patrick Baudry"), another CNES astronaut, flew on that mission). During 1984–1985, he participated in mission training at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center").

Chrétien made his second space flight as a research cosmonaut on board [Soyuz TM-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-7 "Soyuz TM-7"), which launched on 26 November 1988. Together with [Alexander Alexandrovich Volkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Alexandrovich_Volkov_(cosmonaut) "Alexander Alexandrovich Volkov (cosmonaut)") and [Sergei Krikalev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Krikalev "Sergei Krikalev"), he linked up with Mir and joined the crew of [Vladimir Titov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Titov_(cosmonaut) "Vladimir Titov (cosmonaut)"), [Musa Manarov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Manarov "Musa Manarov") and [Valeriy Polyakov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valeriy_Polyakov "Valeriy Polyakov") already on board. They spent 22 days carrying out a program of joint Soviet-French experiments, including a 5-hour and 57-minute EVA by Volkov and Chrétien during which the two men installed the French ERA experimental deployable structure and a panel of material samples. In making the EVA, he became the first non-American and non-Soviet to walk in space. In addition, he was the first non-Soviet cosmonaut to make a second space flight aboard a Soviet spacecraft. The mission lasted 24 days, 18 hours, and 7 minutes.

During 1990–1993, Chrétien participated in [Buran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Buran "Shuttle Buran") spacecraft pilot training at the Moscow Joukovski Institute.

In 1994, he was selected as part of [NASA Astronaut Group 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Group_15 "NASA Astronaut Group 15") to officially become an International Mission Specialist with NASA.

Chrétien attended ASCAN Training at the Johnson Space Center during 1995. He was initially assigned to work on technical issues for the Operations Planning Branch of the Astronaut Office. He served on the crew of [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86")[_Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") (25 September to 6 October 1997) the seventh mission to rendezvous and dock with the Russian Space Station Mir. Highlights included the delivery of a Mir [attitude control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_attitude_control "Spacecraft attitude control") computer, the exchange of U.S. crew members [Mike Foale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Foale "Michael Foale") and [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"), a spacewalk by [Scott E. Parazynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski "Scott E. Parazynski") and Vladimir Titov to retrieve four experiments first deployed on Mir during the [STS-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-76 "STS-76") docking mission, the transfer to Mir of 4,700 kg (10,400 lb) of science and logistics, and the return of experiment hardware and results to [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Mission duration was 10 days, 19 hours, and 21 minutes.

In September 2000, while visiting a [Home Depot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Depot "Home Depot") store in [Webster, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webster,_Texas "Webster, Texas"), he was hit by a 31 kg (68 lb) drill press that fell from a shelf more than 3 m (9.8 ft) above him. The injuries to his neck, head, and shoulders were severe enough that a NASA flight surgeon determined that Chrétien could no longer fly. He was forced to retire from the space program in 2001. He filed a US$15 million lawsuit against Home Depot several months after the accident. The company settled the suit in 2002. The terms of the settlement are protected by a confidentiality agreement.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Loup_Chr%C3%A9tien#cite_note-3) Chrétien is currently working for Tietronix Software as the vice president of research and development in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), Texas.

**Soyuz T-6** was a [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight "Human spaceflight") to Earth orbit to the [Salyut 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_7 "Salyut 7") space station in 1982.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-mirhh-1) Along with two Soviet cosmonauts, the crew included a Frenchman, Jean-Loup Chrétien.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-mirhh-1)

The [Soyuz-T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz-T "Soyuz-T") spacecraft arrived at Salyut 7 following launch on 24 June 1982 and one day of solo operations. During the T-6 mission's time docked to the station, the crew performed joint [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")-French experiments, including [cardiovascular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_heart "Human heart")[echography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ultrasonography "Medical ultrasonography"), alongside the station's [resident crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-5 "Soyuz T-5").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-spacefacts-2)

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soyuz_T-6&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

Soyuz T-6 launched from the [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome") on 24 June 1982 at 16:29 GMT. Docking with the Salyut 7 station was completed manually after problems arose with the spacecraft's onboard automatic docking systems.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-spacefacts-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-astronautix-3)

Once aboard Salyut 7, the crew completed joint Soviet-French, including [echography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ultrasonography "Medical ultrasonography") and [antibiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibiotic "Antibiotic") experiments, with the station's resident crew, the crew of [Soyuz T-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-5 "Soyuz T-5").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-esa1-4)

The mission transported the first French astronaut, Jean-Loup Chrétien, into space. While aboard the station, the resident crew afforded him the opportunity to eject Salyut 7's weekly bag of waste into space through the station's small trash airlock. [Valentin Lebedev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_Lebedev "Valentin Lebedev"), writing in his diary, quoted Chrétien as saying Salyut 7 "is simple, doesn't look impressive, but is reliable."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-mirhh-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-astronautix-3)

## Spacecraft location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soyuz_T-6&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Spacecraft location")]

The Soyuz T-6 reentry capsule is on permanent display at the [Musée de l'air et de l'espace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'air_et_de_l'espace "Musée de l'air et de l'espace"), an aerospace museum at the [Paris–Le Bourget Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Le_Bourget_Airport "Paris–Le Bourget Airport"), north of Paris, France.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-5)

**Soyuz T-6** was a [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight "Human spaceflight") to Earth orbit to the [Salyut 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_7 "Salyut 7") space station in 1982.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-mirhh-1) Along with two Soviet cosmonauts, the crew included a Frenchman, Jean-Loup Chrétien.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-mirhh-1)

The [Soyuz-T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz-T "Soyuz-T") spacecraft arrived at Salyut 7 following launch on 24 June 1982 and one day of solo operations. During the T-6 mission's time docked to the station, the crew performed joint [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")-French experiments, including [cardiovascular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_heart "Human heart")[echography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ultrasonography "Medical ultrasonography"), alongside the station's [resident crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-5 "Soyuz T-5").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-spacefacts-2)

## Mission highlights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soyuz_T-6&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mission highlights")]

Soyuz T-6 launched from the [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome") on 24 June 1982 at 16:29 GMT. Docking with the Salyut 7 station was completed manually after problems arose with the spacecraft's onboard automatic docking systems.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-spacefacts-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-astronautix-3)

Once aboard Salyut 7, the crew completed joint Soviet-French, including [echography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ultrasonography "Medical ultrasonography") and [antibiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibiotic "Antibiotic") experiments, with the station's resident crew, the crew of [Soyuz T-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-5 "Soyuz T-5").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-esa1-4)

The mission transported the first French astronaut, Jean-Loup Chrétien, into space. While aboard the station, the resident crew afforded him the opportunity to eject Salyut 7's weekly bag of waste into space through the station's small trash airlock. [Valentin Lebedev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_Lebedev "Valentin Lebedev"), writing in his diary, quoted Chrétien as saying Salyut 7 "is simple, doesn't look impressive, but is reliable."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-mirhh-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-astronautix-3)

## Spacecraft location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soyuz_T-6&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Spacecraft location")]

The Soyuz T-6 reentry capsule is on permanent display at the [Musée de l'air et de l'espace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'air_et_de_l'espace "Musée de l'air et de l'espace"), an aerospace museum at the [Paris–Le Bourget Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Le_Bourget_Airport "Paris–Le Bourget Airport"), north of Paris, France.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_T-6#cite_note-5)

CNES astronaut Michel Tognini works with a nitrogen freezer on the [STS-93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-93 "STS-93") Space Shuttle mission, which supported the Plant Growth Investigations in Microgravity (PGIM) and Biological Research in Canisters (BRIC) experiments on this mission which took place in 1999. This mission also launched the Chandra X-ray telescope.

**Michel Ange-Charles Tognini** (born 30 September 1949 in [Vincennes, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincennes,_France "Vincennes, France")) is a French [test pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_pilot "Test pilot"), [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer"), brigadier general in the [French Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Air_Force "French Air Force"), and a former [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES") and [ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESA "ESA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") who served from 1 January 2005 to 1 November 2011 as head of the European Astronaut Centre of the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency"). A veteran of two space flights, Tognini has logged a total of 19 days in space. Tognini has 4000 flight hours on 80 types of aircraft (mainly fighter aircraft, including the [MiG-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiG-25 "MiG-25"), [Tupolev Tu-154](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupolev_Tu-154 "Tupolev Tu-154"), [Lightning MK-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_MK-3?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lightning MK-3 (page does not exist)") and [MK-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_MK-5?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lightning MK-5 (page does not exist)"), [Gloster Meteor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloster_Meteor "Gloster Meteor"), and [F-104](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-104 "F-104")). He is fluent in English and [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Tognini was born on 30 September 1949 in [Vincennes, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincennes,_France "Vincennes, France"). Following graduation from [Lycée de Cachan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Maximilien_Sorre "Lycée Maximilien Sorre") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), He attended EPA Grenoble military school (French: _École des pupilles de l'air 749 Grenoble-Montbonnot_) and then went on to study at the [Ecole de l'Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecole_de_l'Air "Ecole de l'Air"), graduating in 1973.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Tognini#cite_note-1)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Following graduation from the academy, Tognini was posted to advanced fighter pilot training at a squadron based at [Normandie-Niemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandie-Niemen "Normandie-Niemen") where he served for one year before obtaining his advanced fighter pilot training. From 1974–1981, he served in the French Air Force as an operational fighter pilot ([Cambrai Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrai_Air_Base?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cambrai Air Base (page does not exist)")), at the 12th Escadre de Chasse, flying SMB2 and [Mirage F1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirage_F1 "Mirage F1") aircraft. During this tour of duty he served as flight leader in 1976, and flight commander in 1979.

In 1982, he was admitted to the _[Empire Test Pilots' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire\_Test\_Pilots'\_School "Empire Test Pilots' School")_ in [Boscombe Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe_Down "Boscombe Down"), United Kingdom, and later that year was awarded his test pilot diploma. He was awarded his military studies diploma in 1983. Tognini was then posted to the [Cazaux Flight Test Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cazaux_Flight_Test_Center?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cazaux Flight Test Center (page does not exist)"), France, initially as a test pilot and subsequently as chief test pilot. During his time there, he helped test a great deal of French flight hardware. He did the weapon systems testing for the [Mirage 2000-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault-Breguet_Mirage_2000 "Dassault-Breguet Mirage 2000"), [Mirage 2000-N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault-Breguet_Mirage_2000N_and_2000D "Dassault-Breguet Mirage 2000N and 2000D"), [Jaguar ATLIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_ATLIS?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jaguar ATLIS (page does not exist)"), and [FLIR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLIR "FLIR") aircraft, and was also responsible for flight safety for pilots, experimenters and flight engineers.

## Astronaut career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Astronaut career")]

In 1985, France opened a recruitment program to expand its astronaut corps, and Tognini was one of seven candidates selected by [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES"). In July 1986, he was one of four candidates to undergo medical examinations in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"). In August 1986, he was assigned as a back-up crew member for the [Soyuz TM-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-7 "Soyuz TM-7") mission. Although Tognini remained a French Air Force officer, he was placed on detachment to [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES") for his space flight activities from September 1986 onwards. In November 1986 he reported to the [Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center"), [Star City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Russia "Star City, Russia"), Russia, for alternate cosmonaut training, including [EVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity"), for the Soviet-French [ARAGATZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARAGATZ?action=edit&redlink=1 "ARAGATZ (page does not exist)") mission.

During 1989–1990 he supported the [Hermes program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermes_(shuttle) "Hermes (shuttle)") in [Toulouse, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse,_France "Toulouse, France").

### Antares

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Antares")]

In 1991 he returned to Star City, Russia, to start prime crew training for the third Soviet-French [ANTARES mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANTARES_mission?action=edit&redlink=1 "ANTARES mission (page does not exist)"). During his stay in Russia, Tognini also gained piloting experience of [BURAN simulators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BURAN_simulators?action=edit&redlink=1 "BURAN simulators (page does not exist)") (MiG-25, Tupolev 154).

Tognini made his first spaceflight on 27 July 1992 aboard [Soyuz TM-15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-15 "Soyuz TM-15") (returning on [Soyuz TM-14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-14 "Soyuz TM-14") on 10 August). Together with [Anatoly Solovyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Solovyev "Anatoly Solovyev") and [Sergei Avdeyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Avdeyev "Sergei Avdeyev") he linked up with [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") (ANTARES mission) and joined the crew of [Alexander Viktorenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Viktorenko "Alexander Viktorenko") and [Alexander Kaleri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Kaleri "Alexander Kaleri") already on board. They spent 14 days carrying out a program of joint Soviet-French experiments before returning to Earth. He returned to France following the mission. During 1993–94, he attended a training cycle of the French [Institute for High Studies of National Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_High_Studies_of_National_Defense "Institute for High Studies of National Defense") (IHEDN).

Tognini attended ASCAN Training at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") during 1995. He was initially assigned to the Operations Planning Branch of the Astronaut Office working technical issues on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), and was subsequently assigned to the Robotics Branch. Tognini was then assigned as ISS [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsule_communicator "Capsule communicator") in [Mission Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Control_Center "Mission Control Center").

### STS-93

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: STS-93")]

Following training at the JSC, Tognini was made available for assignment as a space shuttle mission specialist.

Tognini flew aboard [Space Shuttle Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on [STS-93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-93 "STS-93") (22–27 July 1999) (STS: Space transportation System). During the five-day mission his primary task was to assist in the deployment of the [Chandra X-Ray Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-Ray_Observatory "Chandra X-Ray Observatory"), and to conduct a spacewalk if needed.

He retired from active astronaut status in May 2003.

After having been Head of the European Astronaut Division, he has been the Head of EAC ( European Astronaut Centre) in Cologne, Germany. Now he is in France working for Human Space Exploration with University and performing speeches for general public. He is also the President of GAMA (Groupe Aéronautique du Ministere de l'Air) and President of Space Conseil.

CNES astronaut Michel Tognini works with a nitrogen freezer on the [STS-93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-93 "STS-93") Space Shuttle mission, which supported the Plant Growth Investigations in Microgravity (PGIM) and Biological Research in Canisters (BRIC) experiments on this mission which took place in 1999. This mission also launched the Chandra X-ray telescope.

**Michel Ange-Charles Tognini** (born 30 September 1949 in [Vincennes, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincennes,_France "Vincennes, France")) is a French [test pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_pilot "Test pilot"), [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer"), brigadier general in the [French Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Air_Force "French Air Force"), and a former [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES") and [ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESA "ESA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") who served from 1 January 2005 to 1 November 2011 as head of the European Astronaut Centre of the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency"). A veteran of two space flights, Tognini has logged a total of 19 days in space. Tognini has 4000 flight hours on 80 types of aircraft (mainly fighter aircraft, including the [MiG-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiG-25 "MiG-25"), [Tupolev Tu-154](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupolev_Tu-154 "Tupolev Tu-154"), [Lightning MK-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_MK-3?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lightning MK-3 (page does not exist)") and [MK-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_MK-5?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lightning MK-5 (page does not exist)"), [Gloster Meteor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloster_Meteor "Gloster Meteor"), and [F-104](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-104 "F-104")). He is fluent in English and [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Tognini was born on 30 September 1949 in [Vincennes, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincennes,_France "Vincennes, France"). Following graduation from [Lycée de Cachan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Maximilien_Sorre "Lycée Maximilien Sorre") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), He attended EPA Grenoble military school (French: _École des pupilles de l'air 749 Grenoble-Montbonnot_) and then went on to study at the [Ecole de l'Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecole_de_l'Air "Ecole de l'Air"), graduating in 1973.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Tognini#cite_note-1)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Following graduation from the academy, Tognini was posted to advanced fighter pilot training at a squadron based at [Normandie-Niemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandie-Niemen "Normandie-Niemen") where he served for one year before obtaining his advanced fighter pilot training. From 1974–1981, he served in the French Air Force as an operational fighter pilot ([Cambrai Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrai_Air_Base?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cambrai Air Base (page does not exist)")), at the 12th Escadre de Chasse, flying SMB2 and [Mirage F1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirage_F1 "Mirage F1") aircraft. During this tour of duty he served as flight leader in 1976, and flight commander in 1979.

In 1982, he was admitted to the _[Empire Test Pilots' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire\_Test\_Pilots'\_School "Empire Test Pilots' School")_ in [Boscombe Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe_Down "Boscombe Down"), United Kingdom, and later that year was awarded his test pilot diploma. He was awarded his military studies diploma in 1983. Tognini was then posted to the [Cazaux Flight Test Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cazaux_Flight_Test_Center?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cazaux Flight Test Center (page does not exist)"), France, initially as a test pilot and subsequently as chief test pilot. During his time there, he helped test a great deal of French flight hardware. He did the weapon systems testing for the [Mirage 2000-C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault-Breguet_Mirage_2000 "Dassault-Breguet Mirage 2000"), [Mirage 2000-N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault-Breguet_Mirage_2000N_and_2000D "Dassault-Breguet Mirage 2000N and 2000D"), [Jaguar ATLIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_ATLIS?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jaguar ATLIS (page does not exist)"), and [FLIR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FLIR "FLIR") aircraft, and was also responsible for flight safety for pilots, experimenters and flight engineers.

## Astronaut career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Astronaut career")]

In 1985, France opened a recruitment program to expand its astronaut corps, and Tognini was one of seven candidates selected by [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES"). In July 1986, he was one of four candidates to undergo medical examinations in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"). In August 1986, he was assigned as a back-up crew member for the [Soyuz TM-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-7 "Soyuz TM-7") mission. Although Tognini remained a French Air Force officer, he was placed on detachment to [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES") for his space flight activities from September 1986 onwards. In November 1986 he reported to the [Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center"), [Star City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Russia "Star City, Russia"), Russia, for alternate cosmonaut training, including [EVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity"), for the Soviet-French [ARAGATZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARAGATZ?action=edit&redlink=1 "ARAGATZ (page does not exist)") mission.

During 1989–1990 he supported the [Hermes program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermes_(shuttle) "Hermes (shuttle)") in [Toulouse, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse,_France "Toulouse, France").

### Antares

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Antares")]

In 1991 he returned to Star City, Russia, to start prime crew training for the third Soviet-French [ANTARES mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANTARES_mission?action=edit&redlink=1 "ANTARES mission (page does not exist)"). During his stay in Russia, Tognini also gained piloting experience of [BURAN simulators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BURAN_simulators?action=edit&redlink=1 "BURAN simulators (page does not exist)") (MiG-25, Tupolev 154).

Tognini made his first spaceflight on 27 July 1992 aboard [Soyuz TM-15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-15 "Soyuz TM-15") (returning on [Soyuz TM-14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-14 "Soyuz TM-14") on 10 August). Together with [Anatoly Solovyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Solovyev "Anatoly Solovyev") and [Sergei Avdeyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Avdeyev "Sergei Avdeyev") he linked up with [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") (ANTARES mission) and joined the crew of [Alexander Viktorenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Viktorenko "Alexander Viktorenko") and [Alexander Kaleri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Kaleri "Alexander Kaleri") already on board. They spent 14 days carrying out a program of joint Soviet-French experiments before returning to Earth. He returned to France following the mission. During 1993–94, he attended a training cycle of the French [Institute for High Studies of National Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_High_Studies_of_National_Defense "Institute for High Studies of National Defense") (IHEDN).

Tognini attended ASCAN Training at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") during 1995. He was initially assigned to the Operations Planning Branch of the Astronaut Office working technical issues on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), and was subsequently assigned to the Robotics Branch. Tognini was then assigned as ISS [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsule_communicator "Capsule communicator") in [Mission Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Control_Center "Mission Control Center").

### STS-93

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michel_Tognini&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: STS-93")]

Following training at the JSC, Tognini was made available for assignment as a space shuttle mission specialist.

Tognini flew aboard [Space Shuttle Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on [STS-93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-93 "STS-93") (22–27 July 1999) (STS: Space transportation System). During the five-day mission his primary task was to assist in the deployment of the [Chandra X-Ray Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-Ray_Observatory "Chandra X-Ray Observatory"), and to conduct a spacewalk if needed.

He retired from active astronaut status in May 2003.

After having been Head of the European Astronaut Division, he has been the Head of EAC ( European Astronaut Centre) in Cologne, Germany. Now he is in France working for Human Space Exploration with University and performing speeches for general public. He is also the President of GAMA (Groupe Aéronautique du Ministere de l'Air) and President of Space Conseil.

**Jean-Pierre Haigneré** (born 19 May 1948) is a [French Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Air_Force "French Air Force") officer and a former [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES")[spationaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spationaut "Spationaut").

Jean-Pierre Haigneré was born in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), France, and joined the French Air Force, where he trained as a test pilot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-1)

He flew on two missions to the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") space station in 1993 and 1999. The [Mir Perseus (Mir EO-27)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Mir_Expeditions "List of Mir Expeditions") long-duration mission (186 days) in 1999 also included an [EVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-2) In addition to his duties at the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency"), Jean-Pierre Haigneré is also involved in a European [space tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tourism "Space tourism") initiative, the _[Astronaute Club Européen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaute\_Club\_Europ%C3%A9en "Astronaute Club Européen")_ (ACE), which he co-founded with Alain Dupas and Laurent Gathier.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-3) He is credited with taking the first picture of the shadow of a [Solar eclipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_eclipse "Solar eclipse") from space. He took this during the [Mir Perseus (Mir EO-27)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Mir_Expeditions "List of Mir Expeditions") mission.

## Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Family")]

He is married to former French astronaut [Claudie Haigneré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudie_Haigner%C3%A9 "Claudie Haigneré").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-4) The [asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[135268 Haigneré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/135268_Haigner%C3%A9 "135268 Haigneré") is named in their combined honour.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-5)

**Jean-Pierre Haigneré** (born 19 May 1948) is a [French Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Air_Force "French Air Force") officer and a former [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES "CNES")[spationaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spationaut "Spationaut").

Jean-Pierre Haigneré was born in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), France, and joined the French Air Force, where he trained as a test pilot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-1)

He flew on two missions to the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") space station in 1993 and 1999. The [Mir Perseus (Mir EO-27)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Mir_Expeditions "List of Mir Expeditions") long-duration mission (186 days) in 1999 also included an [EVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-2) In addition to his duties at the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space Agency"), Jean-Pierre Haigneré is also involved in a European [space tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tourism "Space tourism") initiative, the _[Astronaute Club Européen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaute\_Club\_Europ%C3%A9en "Astronaute Club Européen")_ (ACE), which he co-founded with Alain Dupas and Laurent Gathier.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-3) He is credited with taking the first picture of the shadow of a [Solar eclipse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_eclipse "Solar eclipse") from space. He took this during the [Mir Perseus (Mir EO-27)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Mir_Expeditions "List of Mir Expeditions") mission.

## Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Family")]

He is married to former French astronaut [Claudie Haigneré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudie_Haigner%C3%A9 "Claudie Haigneré").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-4) The [asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[135268 Haigneré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/135268_Haigner%C3%A9 "135268 Haigneré") is named in their combined honour.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Haigner%C3%A9#cite_note-5)
